articles.title: Turn a list of prospect websites into honest page-speed reports for outreach
articles.excerpt: A cold email saying "your website is slow" gets deleted. One saying "your services page takes N seconds to show its main content on a phone, and two fixes would shorten that" gets read, because the ow…
articles.body: A cold email saying "your website is slow" gets deleted. One saying "your services page takes N seconds to show its main content on a phone, and two fixes would shorten that" gets read, because the owner can check it. Below: pages to pick, four numbers, a ranking script and the etiquette. Google's PageSpeed Insights API does the measuring; PageSpeed Insights Audit is an Apify Actor that runs it over a list of URLs. Pick the pages that matter Audit three or four pages per prospect, chosen as a customer would use the site: The homepage, because the owner has seen it. The page that earns money: the main service, product or booking page. One page that attracts visitors, such as a popular blog post. The contact or checkout page. Use mobile, since Google Search ranks with mobile data.

articles.title: AI Chatbot Refund Policy: Stop Disputes Before They Start
articles.excerpt: An agent that promises a refund it cannot authorize turns a support tool into a liability. Here are the six cases it must always escalate and the rule wording it can actually follow. At 9:12 p.m. a cu…
articles.body: An agent that promises a refund it cannot authorize turns a support tool into a liability. Here are the six cases it must always escalate and the rule wording it can actually follow. At 9:12 p.m. a customer typed one line into a website chat: can I get a refund? The agent answered two seconds later: "Of course — I've approved a full refund and it will be back on your card within 3–5 days." The agent had no refund authority and no way to issue one. The business found out three days later, when the customer pasted that message back and asked where their money was. One sentence, sent at night, with nobody watching. The six cases that must always escalate An agent should never decide any of the following on its own.

articles.title: We open-sourced the tool that failed its own kill rule
articles.excerpt: Before we ran the experiment, we wrote down the rule that would kill it. The product under test was a pipeline that builds skill files for AI agents: those structured instruction documents, SKILL.md a…
articles.body: Before we ran the experiment, we wrote down the rule that would kill it. The product under test was a pipeline that builds skill files for AI agents: those structured instruction documents, SKILL.md and friends, that tell an agent when to trigger, what to do, and what never to do. Our hypothesis was the obvious one. Skills built through a structured pipeline, with a requirements interview, controlled generation, and a mechanical audit, should beat skills the model improvises for itself in one shot. We pre-registered four predictions and one kill criterion: if the pipeline could not measurably beat one-shot generation, we would say so in public and change the product. Then we ran it.

articles.body: AI agents need small facts all the time: a token balance, a company's filing, a page as clean text, a weather alert. Most APIs make an agent sign up, store a key and buy a plan first. SiteCheck works the other way. Each tool is one HTTP endpoint with a price between $0.001 and $0.01. The agent calls it, gets an HTTP 402 with the price, pays in USDC on Base, Solana or Arc with the x402 protocol, and gets the answer. No account, no API key, no subscription. If the upstream source fails, the call is not charged.

articles.title: Why You Should Understand Machine Learning and GPT Technology Before You Start Prompting Your AI
articles.excerpt: Most of us met large language models through a chat box. You type something, it answers, and it feels like talking to a very well-read colleague. That feeling is useful, and it is also the source of m…
articles.body: Most of us met large language models through a chat box. You type something, it answers, and it feels like talking to a very well-read colleague. That feeling is useful, and it is also the source of most of the frustration developers run into later. The model is not a colleague. It is a statistical system with specific habits, and once you know those habits, your prompts get better, your agents get more predictable, and your token bill gets smaller. This article is about those habits. A quick note on where this came from You don't need a history lesson, but three moments explain most of what follows. In 2017, Google researchers published Attention Is All You Need , introducing the transformer architecture.

articles.title: Missing Intune apps? Force a Company Portal sync before you reinstall
articles.excerpt: A common help desk ticket: the user enrolled their work laptop, but the required apps or configuration policies never showed up. Before you wipe the device or reinstall Company Portal, force an Intune…
articles.body: A common help desk ticket: the user enrolled their work laptop, but the required apps or configuration policies never showed up. Before you wipe the device or reinstall Company Portal, force an Intune check-in. Many of these tickets are just a delayed sync. Why this happens Intune does not push every change the second an admin assigns an app. Devices check in on a schedule. If the user just enrolled, was offline, or the assignment was added after enrollment, the PC may still be waiting for its next check-in. A manual sync asks the device to talk to Intune now. Steps on the device On the Windows PC, open Company Portal (search for it in the Start menu). Open Settings , or go to the device details and look for Check status / Sync . Start the sync and wait a few minutes.

Google talks a big game about trying to keep the Android ecosystem safe and secure. The company recently started cracking down on sideloading apps because malicious actors can easily create fake apps and trick users into installing them. articles.title: Four years ago, NASA punched an asteroid. Europe's Hera probe arrives this month to inspect the wreckage
articles.excerpt: NASA's DART mission made a cosmic mess four years ago — and now a new spacecraft is ready to scout out exactly what the first-of-its-kind collision accomplished.
articles.body: NASA's DART mission made a cosmic mess four years ago — and now a new spacecraft is ready to scout out exactly what the first-of-its-kind collision accomplished. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft slammed into a small space rock called Dimorphos on Sept. 26, 2022, in humanity's first test of planetary defense. That's the field dedicated to protecting Earth from the possibility of a calamitous asteroid impact, and DART mimicked how humans could change the orbit of a threatening space rock, taking it off its collision course. The mission definitely succeeded, shortening the little asteroid's orbit around a larger rock called Didymos by about 33 minutes .

articles.body: Now you see them, now you don't. Scientists have discovered that some of the universe's most powerful explosions, hypernovas, may not happen at all. These explosions, known as hypernovas , were first proposed to explain unusual stars in the halo of our galaxy, the Milky Way , and in a neighboring dwarf galaxy. It was suggested that these stars could only form from the debris of an explosion 10 times more powerful than the 'average' supernovas . The team behind these new findings suggests that ordinary supernovas could actually account for these stars when the uneven or non-spherical way they fling out matter is considered. "If we look at a supernova today, the star's materials are not spread evenly. Oxygen might predominantly fly in one direction, sulphur in another.

articles.body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 October 14 – Mars… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Mars and the Beehive Under an Aurora Explanation: What a cosmic coincidence! In today’s image , Mars joins the Beehive cluster ( M44 or Praesepe) below an auroral curtain and above a horizon of happy little trees near Lansjärv, Sweden . An eruption off the Sun reached Earth on October 10th, 2026 causing strong disturbances in Earth’s magnetic field .

articles.body: An OpenAI engineer was arrested after the company said it discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in one of its offices. The employee was identified as Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national. Alfozan is charged with using or endeavoring to use a device to intercept oral communications, according to a press release from the Department of Justice . OpenAI's post about the incident says it used its AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier."
